items.title: 0. Introduction
items.text: This documentation specifies the standards for MakeACS and MakeACS-compatible hardware, to ensure proper interoperability between components.

items.title: What is MakeACS?
items.text:
MakeACS is an open-source set of hardware, software, and standards for a simple, versatile shop management and access control system. Originally developed at the Rochester Insitute of Technology, this system provides many automations to assist in the management and oversight of makerspaces, Fab Labs, teaching shops, etc.

The hardware is primarily for machine-level access control, statistics collection, and shop automation. Users are permitted to only use equipment they are authorized to use (based on trainings, staff sign-offs, SSO credential information, etc.), and their usage (or failure to use) equipment is logged for statistical analysis, or to automatically inform things like maintenance tickets based on usage.

The server is where users, staff, and the hardware communicate. The server incorporates a training management and serving system for safety and competency trainings (as well as the ability to API-integrate with other services), centralized inventory, maintenance, usage, and staff tracking, and an MQTT API for the hardware deployed in the shop.

The hardware and server are both designed to be easy to adapt without the other, with well-defined, open-ended APIs for all interactions.

This documentation will focus specifically on the hardware, but more information on MakeACS in general, or of a specific aspect of it, can be found in the MakeACS GitHub.

items.title: Terminology
items.text:
• Deployment : All physically interconnected pieces of MakeACS hardware.
  • Component : A single piece of MakeACS hardware.
  • Core : The master of a MakeACS deployment. There is only one, and it serves as the primary point of communication out of the deployment.
  • Switch : A MakeACS component intended to control access to a device, by interrupting its normal operation in some way.

items.title: Topology
items.text: A MakeACS deployment can be made of one to many components, but the general topology is always the same; * A deployment must exactly one Core. * The Core always makes up one end of the MakeACS deployment's topology. * Further MakeACS components can be connected to the Core via the standard interface. * Some MakeACS components are passthrough, meaning there is a standard interface on both sides to allow further connection of another device. * Some MakeACS components are terminating, meaning there is only one standard interface to connect with. * Some MakeACS components are splitting, meaning there is one input and multiple outputs, allowing the fanout of the deployment. In most scenarios, the most common deployment is one Core connected to one Switch, sometimes with a passthrough component in the center.

items.title: Table of Contents
items.text: 1. Introduction

items.title: Component Connector
items.text:
The standard interface connector is the most important aspect of a MakeACS component, and is what ensures interoperability with all other components in a deployment.

The MakeACS standard connector is an HD15, with components always having the female receptacle side. To prevent confusion with VGA or SVGA connections, blue receptacles, housings, cables, wiring harnesses, etc. are not permitted in a MakeACS deployment.

Warning

The HD15 used by MakeACS is the same physical connector as a VGA or SVGA video signal, but plugging in a video cable to the MakeACS bus can damage the computer or monitor!

items.title: Component Interconnect
items.text: For connecting components, high-quality HD15 cables are to be used. The suggested ones for use with MakeACS are those manufactured by Amphenol Cables on Demand. Cables must meet the following criteria; * Length of no more than 25 feet. * Fully shielded, with shield connections to both connectors. * Positive retention screws on both sides of both connectors. * Wire gauge of 26 AWG or larger on all conductors. * No combined conductors.

items.title: Power
items.text:
See power for more information.

Ground (3, 10, 11, 14) : Primary system ground, all power and signal is referenced to this ground level.

12 Volt Bus (4, 5) : Nominal 12v power for component use. Designs should be able to handle sustained 2 amps.

5 Volt Bus (6, 13) : Nominal 5v power for component use. Designs should be able to handle sustained 2 amps.

items.title: Standard Signals
items.text:
Access (1) : Digital signal, originates at the Core. 5v logic level, 30mA nominal drive strength, push-pull. This signal is the primary logical signal to indicate if a deployment should grant access to its equipment. Components that make use of this signal must have a user-visible LED that indicates when the signal is present, for debug purposes. This LED must be yellow.

OneWire (2) : Open-drain bidirectional digital signal, pulled to 5v by the Core. 1mA nominal pull-up strength. This bus is used for enumeration and identification of components in a deployment, and informs the operation of the Core. See Component ID for more information.

Interrupt (7) : Open-drain bidirectional digital signal, pulled to 5v by the Core. 5mA nominal pull-up strength. This signal can be pulled low by any component to indicate that the deployment should be put into a suspended state (i.e. revoke access, do not approve access). The Core has the ability to pull this low as well, as a way to inform other components that the deployment is currently locked out or otherwise unavailable. Components capable of generating an Interrupt signal must have a user-visible LED that indicates the device is in an interrupt state. This LED must be red.

items.title: Application-Defined Signals
items.text:
See GPIO for more information.

GPIO 1 (8) : Application-defined input/output #1.

GPIO 2 (9) : Application-defined input/output #2.

GPIO 3 (12) : Application-defined input/output #3.

GPIO 4 (15) : Application-defined input/output #4.

items.title: Shield
items.text: The shield of all cables must be connected together with a large, continuous copper connection within each component that has more than one HD15 connector. All components leave the shield floating except for the Core, which ties it to ground for shielding and EMI purposes.

items.title: Reduced Connector Standard (MakeACS-Lite)
items.text:
For components that do not need or cannot fit the standard HD15 connector, and to allow for backwards-compatibility with the previous SMACS Hardware Standard, a reduced-pin interface is also standardized. Signals have the same voltage level and drive characteristics as they would in the HD15 connector. The DB9 shield is treated the same as the HD15 shield (i.e. grounded at the Core, floating otherwise).

  1. Access
  2. OneWire
  3. Ground
  4. 5 Volt Power
  5. Ground
  6. 5 Volt Power
  7. Interrupt
  8. Unused (Float, RFU)
  9. Ground

Warning

SMACS-compliant hardware will likely have issues related to power when used with the MakeACS Reduced Connector Standard, for the following reasons;

  • SMACS has a Schottky diode inline with each 5v power output pin, making effective bus power closer to 4.3-4.5v.
  • SMACS 5v rail is limited at 500mA maximum current, compared to MakeACS 1000mA minimum current.
  • SMACS does not connect pin 9 of the DB9, resulting in higher voltage losses across the line.
  • SMACS uses pin 6 as a "Type" identifier", resulting in much higher voltage drop across the line.

When using a SMACS component with a MakeACS Core or similar, supplementary power for the Core may be required.

The pinout of the Reduced Connector Standard is chosen such that off-the-shelf HD15 to DB9 adapters, generally meant for CGA or MultiSync to VGA conversion, will properly adapt between the connections.

items.title: Application-Specific Connectors
items.text: Deviations from the connector standard are permitted where it makes for a more reliable, easier-to-use, or much less expensive component. However, a means to convert the component's deviation back to a standard HD15 must always be included. A common example is to have DIN rail-mounted switch that has bare screw terminals to connect to the MakeACS bus, so an HD15 to bare-wire cable can be more easily passed through the electrical box's cable glands for installation.

items.title: Bridging Deployments
items.text: There are situations where connecting two deployments is necessary. When this happens, a dedicated interconnecting component must be used, that arbitrates the signals. Only the ground, power rails, and interrupt lines may be connected across the deployments directly.

items.title: 2. Power
items.text: One of the main benefits of MakeACS is the decentralized power. In most deployments, the power required to operate the system can be harvested directly by the Switches to power the Core and other components.

items.title: Power Rails
items.text:
The MakeACS bus has two power rails; a nominal 12 volt one and a nominal 5 volt one. Both power rails are rated for up to 2 amps each.

The 12 volt rail is generically the high-power rail. Components may supply any voltage they have available between 9 and 12 volts to this rail. The 5 volt rail has tighter control for logic-level operation, and components cannot provide anything outside of 4.8 to 5.2 volts to this rail.

The Core is required to provide a regulator that will make available at least 1 amp on the 5 volt rail from the 12 volt rail, for deployment where there are 12 volt supplying devices but no 5 volt supplying devices.

Components may use the 12 volt rail for high-current applications like large lights, displays, motors, etc., while the 5 volt rail is reserved for minimal draw to power logical circuitry. Any component with sustained 5 volt loads in excess of 250mA should implement their own regulator from the 12 volt rail.

items.title: Rail Connections
items.text: Rails operates as a decentralized ideal diode OR. All power-supplying components attaching to the rail are required to do so though an ideal diode, such that power supplies can load share or dynamically be replaced as they are superseded or removed from the bus. Reference components for this application are the MX66100T for low-current (USB or similar) implementations, and the MX5052S for most other implementations.

items.title: Supply Requirements
items.text:
Any component that is capable of supplying power is required do to do, and must provide as much as possible (up to the 2 amp limit) to the bus. If a device is capable of supplying its own power, it must prioritize the use of its own power for internal operation where possible.

It is the responsibility of the power-supplying component to protect itself and its power-supplying circuitry from overcurrents in excess of what it is rated for. A self-recovering overcurrent protection, such as a polyfuse/self-healing fuse or eFuse (preferred) are required for this current limiting. Reference component for this application is the MX25947ES.

When a component implements an open-ended connection for an external supply that does not have a well-established voltage level, such as a barrel jack, the component must implement over- and under-voltage protection to avoid damage to the deployment. Reference component for this application is the MX25947ES.

Power suppliers that are not inherently powered by their normal use (i.e. requires an additional, external connection to power) but require that external power to operate properly must implement hardware to pull down the Interrupt pin when there is an invalid power connection.

items.title: Consumer Requirements
items.text:
Power consuming components are required to implement a polyfuse/self-healing fuse on their input, to protect the deployment at-large from a short inside of that component.

Power consumers can require the presence of the 12v rail before operating. If this is the case, the power consumer must implement hardware to pull down the Interrupt rail when there is no 12v power present.

Components can assume the 5v rail is always present, since it is provided by the Core. The lack of a present 5v rail is considered an invalid state, and components are not expected to operate in this scenario.

items.title: Indicators
items.text: All components are required to have user-visible LED indicators of their power state. This LED must be green. The LED must be able to indicate that all requires power rails are present and working. An LED on each the 5v and 12v rail is permissible, or a single LED lit by the combination of the two.

items.title: 3. Component ID
items.text:
All MakeACS components except for the Core are required to implement a OneWire device on the OneWire pin of the bus. The reference device for this purpose is the UMW DS18B20Z.

This OneWire device is used for 3 main purposes;

  • It provides a globally unique identifier for the component, which is used both for bus integrity checks (see Unique Identifier) and communicative device enumeration (see GPIO).
  • It provides a device type and classification to inform the Core how to operate (see Device Classification).

  • It provides regular temperature monitoring of the deployment to look for anomalous conditions.

  • Generic Device

  • Generic Device II
  • Communicative Device
  • 2Ch Device
  • 3Ch Device
  • 4Ch Device

items.title: Memory Structure
items.text:
The DS18B20 and similar OneWire temperature sensors have a high-temperature and low-temperature threshold that is stored in persistent EEPROM. This EEPROM is repurposed on MakeACS in the following schema;

Byte Bit Purpose T-HIGH 7 CLASS 2 T-HIGH 6 CLASS 1 T-HIGH 5 CLASS 0 T-HIGH 4 UNIQUE 12 T-HIGH 3 UNIQUE 11 T-HIGH 2 UNIQUE 10 T-HIGH 1 UNIQUE 9 T-HIGH 0 UNIQUE 8 T-LOW 7 UNIQUE 7 T-LOW 6 UNIQUE 6 T-LOW 5 UNIQUE 5 T-LOW 4 UNIQUE 4 T-LOW 3 UNIQUE 3 T-LOW 2 UNIQUE 2 T-LOW 1 UNIQUE 1 T-LOW 0 UNIQUE 0

See Device Classification for information on the 3 "CLASS" bits.

See Type Identifier for information on the 13 "UNIQUE" bits.

items.title: Device Classification
items.text:
To inform the Core as to what types of the components make up a deployment, every component is given a classification. The classification is one of 8 options, as seen in the following table;

Bits Role 000 Communicative 001 General Purpose 010 General Purpose 011 General Purpose 100 General Purpose 101 2 Channel 110 3 Channel 111 4 Channel

Communicative components can interface with the Core via a higher-level communication protocol. See GPIO for more information.

Generic Components are generic components that do not take advantage of the GPIO. These may be 1-channel Switches (switched directly off the Access signal), passive devices that just monitor the bus (like a status light), or a monitoring device that asserts the Interrupt (like a temperature sensor).

2, 3, and 4 Channel are Switches that use the GPIO to switch multiple outputs, i.e. a 4 Channel Switch has 4 outputs, and when Access and GPIO 1 are both high, output 1 is active. See GPIO for more information.

items.title: Type Identifier
items.text:
In addition to the 3 bit Device Classification, every device has a 13 bit Type Identifier. The Type Identifier allows for the Core to identify the model/series of component it is connected to, by referencing the MakeACS Components Table.

Type Identifiers are issued sequentially in each Device Classification.

items.title: Unique Identifier
items.text:
OneWire devices inherently have a globally unique 64-bit identifier, which is used by MakeACS to verify the composition of the deployment.

The Core will monitor for the presence of the expected Unique Identifiers, and if one is missing, or an unexpected one is found, it raises a fault condition until cleared by an authorized user, indicating to re-seal the deployment as-is.

items.title: 4. GPIO
items.text:
To allow for more versatile, powerful, and application-specific deployments, the MakeACS connector provisions four open-ended GPIO whose use is assigned based on the detected composition of the deployment (see Component ID).

All four GPIO are able to operate as either a Schmitt trigger input or 30mA push-pull output at a 5 volt logic level. The Core can dynamically swap between input and output mode to also achieve a Hi-Z "output" state.

Currently, two forms of GPIO operation are supported:

  • Multi-Channel Switches allow for up to 4 independent control channels to be activated by the Core.
  • Communicative Components can communicate with the Core via a standard, higher-level communication protocol.

Warning

Communicative Components are mutually exclusive with Multi-Channel Switches.

General Purpose Components (1 Channel Switches, etc.) can be used with either GPIO-using component type.

items.title: Multi-Channel Switches
items.text:
Multi-Channel Switches are the primary use of the MakeACS GPIO. These allow for up to 4 independent control channels to be activated by the Core, based on different permission levels of the user. As a practical example, this would allow for a single Core to control an entire electronics workbench; it always turns on the power supply and multimeter when someone attempts to access it, but the soldering iron and hot-air rework gun can each be behind their own separate trainings.

When operating as a Multi-Channel Switch, the GPIO number maps to the access control channel, i.e. a 2 Channel Switch would use GPIO 1 and 2 to determine access, and GPIO 3 and 4 are undefined. The Switch must hardware AND the GPIO signal with the Core's main Access signal, such that the loss of either immediately shuts down the output channel.

Warning

To prevent unexpected behavior, a deployment cannot have more than one Multi-Channel Switch.

Note

While the standard is designed to allow for multi-channel components whose channels are set via communication instead of GPIO, it is not supported at this time.

items.title: Communicative Components
items.text:
In addition to generic digital signals, the GPIO can be used for higher-level communication between components and the Core. This enables the sending of more complex data, triggering API calls, or setting up more complex logic for a component to achieve a specific goal.

For more information on the data formatting and structure used, see Bus Communication.

items.title: Half-Duplex Mode
items.text:
Half-Duplex Mode allows for one or multiple Communicative Components to communicate with the Core in a shared bus via half duplex RS485. The pinout is as follows;

  • GPIO 1 : RS485 Non-Inverting Input/Output
  • GPIO 2 : RS485 Inverting Input/Output
  • GPIO 3 : Open-Drain Interrupt. Pulled up at the Core (5mA nominal at 5 volts), Components can drive it low to indicate an urgent message.
  • GPIO 4 : Push-Pull Suspend/Reset. Driven by the Core, when low all Communicative Components are expected to enter a suspended state. On the high-going transition of this signal, Components are expected to resume operation in a reset state. This signal is used to fix hanging/broken Components, and to perform regular restarts to clear memory fragmentation.

items.title: Full-Duplex Mode
items.text:
Full-Duplex Mode allows for one high-bandwidth component to communicate exclusively with the Core.

At this time, there are no use-cases for the Full-Duplex mode that the standard allows for, so no standards are developed.

items.title: 5. Bus Communication
items.text:
This page details the communication structure used for Communicative Components to interact with the Core. For more information on Communicative Components, see GPIO.

Info

At this time, only the Half-Duplex communication standard is implemented. Full-Duplex standards will be developed when a valid use-case for them arises.
